title: Research, Inc. v. United States
articleTitle: The Jurisprudence of Incremental Innovation: A Comprehensive Analysis of Research, Inc. v. United States and the Evolution of Federal R&D Tax Credit Compliance
court: United States District Court, District of Minnesota
subject: Substantiation of Base Period Research Expenses
summary: Research, Inc. v. United States (D. Minn. 1995) is a key federal R&D tax credit case for U.S. taxpayers claiming the research credit. The court denied a $404,237 refund because Research, Inc. claimed "special system projects" in its 1985 credit year but could not substantiate matching base period expenses, proving base period records and consistency are essential.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Genesis

In the jurisprudence governing the United States federal credit for increasing research activities, Research, Inc. v. United States, Civ. No. 3-94-385 (also docketed as No. 3-93-CIV-742), 95-1 USTC ¶ 50,407, 95-2 USTC ¶ 50,407, 76 AFTR 2d 95-5688, 1995 WL 560140 (D. Minn. June 21, 1995), stands as a foundational judicial authority on base period substantiation and a direct precursor to the statutory consistency mandate that Congress codified in 1989, after the tax year at issue. Adjudicated in the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota, the dispute arose from a tax refund suit initiated by Research, Inc., a Minnesota-based engineering and manufacturing corporation, seeking a refund of $404,237 attributable to additional federal research and development (R&D) tax credits for its fiscal taxable year ending September 30, 1985.

During the taxable year at issue, Research, Inc. designed, manufactured, and sold control instrumentation and heating devices, offering both a standard line of products and several "special system projects"—prototype systems designed and constructed to meet the specialized needs and requirements of individual customers. On its original 1985 return, the taxpayer claimed $1,881,143 in qualified research expenses (QREs) attributable solely to its standard product line; it then filed an amended return claiming an additional $1,667,717 in QREs attributable to its "special system projects" (which the court also called "unique systems"), an amount that would have qualified it for an additional $413,972 in research credit. While the taxpayer sought to include the costs of these "special system projects" in its 1985 credit year computation, it failed to include the corresponding research expenses for "special system projects" in its historical base period computations, which reflected only standard-product-line QREs of $1,426,165, $1,772,137, and $1,857,538 for fiscal years 1982, 1983, and 1984, an average (base period research expense) of $1,685,280. Crucially, the record before the court on the Government's motion for summary judgment established, and the taxpayer did not dispute, that it had engaged in developing "special system projects" in each of the three base period years preceding the 1985 credit year. However, the taxpayer had destroyed the relevant documentation of its qualified research expenses for 1982, 1983, and 1984, or was otherwise unable to produce it, and conceded that it could not produce an accurate accounting of the base period research expenses attributable to its "special system projects".
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The United States Department of Justice, Tax Division, together with the Office of the United States Attorney, representing the United States, challenged the refund claim on computational, statutory, and evidentiary grounds by moving for summary judgment. The Government contended that the language and intent of former I.R.C. § 30 provide a credit only for increasing research expenditures over base period research expenses. Because Research, Inc. claimed the costs of its "special system projects" in the 1985 credit year without adjusting its base period expenses to reflect its expenditures on the same unique product line during the base years—and admitted that it could not do so—the Government argued that the taxpayer could not accurately delineate its base period amounts, leaving no indicia of the amount of any increase in research spending.

Furthermore, the Government's position, which the court adopted, rested on the principle that deductions and tax credits are matters of legislative grace, so the taxpayer bears the burden of proving that it complies with every requirement of the statute, including the correct amount of its base period research expenses; the court grounded that burden in authorities such as New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, Helvering v. Taylor, Welch v. Helvering, and Lewis v. Reynolds, and its opinion does not cite I.R.C. § 6001 or the regulations thereunder. Because Research, Inc. had destroyed, or was otherwise unable to produce, the records necessary to establish its base period QREs for the "special system projects," the Government asserted that the taxpayer was not entitled to any additional refund and, indeed, was not entitled to the research credit at all. The Government also conceded that there was no authoritative basis for a retroactive recomputation of the base period years—which were closed, and which the IRS had refused to let the taxpayer adjust during a 1988 audit of the 1985 return—but maintained that recomputation was not the issue; the issue was the taxpayer's failure to produce an accurate accounting of its base period expenses. The $404,237 refund sought was itself predicated on a hypothecated upward adjustment of $396,801 to the base period expense figure, derived from a "sales ratio" calculated by the Government's examiner during a 1990 audit of the amended return, for which the court found no basis in law or fact.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The court's analysis in Research, Inc. v. United States rested on the plain terms of the substantive incremental credit mechanics of former I.R.C. § 30 and on general burden-of-proof principles governing tax refund suits; the opinion does not discuss the federal tax recordkeeping mandates, although those mandates supply important context for practitioners. To appreciate the full legal weight of the ruling, tax practitioners must trace the statutory continuity from the code provisions in effect for fiscal year 1985 to the modern regime under I.R.C. § 41.

The federal research credit was originally enacted by Congress as part of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA), Pub. L. No. 97-34, § 221, 95 Stat. 172, 241–247 (1981), and codified at former I.R.C. § 44F. The legislative history to the 1981 enactment explicitly states that Congress designed an incremental credit to overcome the reluctance of ongoing businesses to bear the significant staffing, supply, and equipment costs required to initiate or expand research programs beyond their normal baseline operations. Under the Tax Reform Act of 1984, Pub. L. No. 98-369, 98 Stat. 494 (1984), Congress recodified former § 44F as former I.R.C. § 30, which was the exact statutory provision governing Research, Inc.'s fiscal year ending September 30, 1985. Subsequently, the Tax Reform Act of 1986, Pub. L. No. 99-514, § 231, 100 Stat. 2085, 2173–2180 (1986), amended and recodified the provision as current I.R.C. § 41.

Under former I.R.C. § 30(a) (and modern I.R.C. § 41(a)(1)), the credit is calculated as a statutory percentage (20 percent under current law; 25 percent under former I.R.C. § 30(a) for the 1985 tax year at issue in Research, Inc.) of the excess of the taxpayer's QREs for the determination year over the taxpayer's base period research expenses (now termed the "base amount"). For the 1985 tax year at issue in Research, Inc., former I.R.C. § 30(c) utilized a "rolling base period" mechanism, defining base period research expenses as the average of the QREs for each year in the base period and the base period as the three taxable years immediately preceding the determination year (for Research, Inc., fiscal years 1982, 1983, and 1984). Under the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 (OBRA 1989), Congress replaced the three-year rolling base period of the Regular Credit with a "fixed-base percentage" under I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(A), defined as the ratio of a taxpayer's aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (subject to a statutory maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent under I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) and a minimum base amount floor of 50 percent of current-year QREs under I.R.C. § 41(c)(2), alongside specialized start-up rules under I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)). Furthermore, for modern taxpayers electing the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) (which ultimately supplanted the former Alternative Incremental Research Credit (AIRC)), the statute utilizes a three-year rolling base period, providing a credit equal to 14 percent of the QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (or a flat 6 percent of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had zero QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years).

Crucially, however, the statutory "Consistency Requirement" did not exist in former I.R.C. § 30(c) as applied to Research, Inc.'s 1985 tax year: as the court expressly noted in footnote 2 of its opinion, the problem presented by the case was subsequently resolved by a 1989 amendment that added the consistency rule—then codified at I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) and applicable to tax years beginning after 1989—which provides that, notwithstanding whether the period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any base year, the QREs taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year; following later redesignations, the rule now appears at current I.R.C. § 41(c)(5) (formerly § 41(c)(6)) and is implemented by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d). Under this mandate, the QREs taken into account in computing the base period (or fixed-base percentage) must be determined on a basis entirely consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year. Complementing this substantive rule is I.R.C. § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), which obligate every taxpayer claiming a tax credit to keep permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the exact amount of gross income, deductions, and credits required to be shown on any return.
The Court's Final Holding

On June 21, 1995, the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota (Judge Michael J. Davis) granted the United States' motion for summary judgment and dismissed the action with prejudice, denying Research, Inc.'s claim for a refund attributable to additional R&D tax credits for the taxable year ending September 30, 1985, in its entirety. The court held that, by the plain terms of former I.R.C. § 30, the taxpayer had to show (1) the amount of its QREs in the determination year, (2) the amount of its QREs for each of the three base years, and (3) that its determination-year QREs exceeded the base period average; because the taxpayer had engaged in developing "special system projects" in each of the base years, it was required to show the QREs attributable to both its unique and standard product lines. Because Research, Inc. had destroyed the relevant documentation or was otherwise unable to produce it, the court concluded that the taxpayer could show neither initial qualification for the credit nor the required increase over the three-year base period average. The failure to substantiate the base period was fatal to the entire credit claim; quoting Justice Holmes, the court observed that "Men must turn square corners when they deal with the Government". In the decades since the ruling, Research, Inc. v. United States has been cited by the IRS—including in its Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide and its Exhibit D computational check sheet—and by practitioners analyzing later decisions such as Union Carbide, United States v. Quebe, and George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, as a leading precedent for disallowing R&D tax credit claims where base period attributes are unsubstantiated or asymmetrically calculated.
Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
Asymmetrical Project Inclusion and Violation of the Consistency Requirement

The primary substantive defect in Research, Inc. v. United States was the taxpayer's failure to carry its burden of proving its base period research expenses on the same project scope it used for the credit year; because the statutory consistency rule had not yet been enacted, the court rested its decision on the plain terms of former I.R.C. § 30 and general burden-of-proof principles rather than on a statutory consistency mandate. Mathematically, the Regular Research Credit under former I.R.C. § 30(a) and current I.R.C. § 41(a)(1) is governed by the incremental formula:
Credit = r × (QREscredit year − Base Amount)

where r represents the statutory credit rate (20 percent under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1); 25 percent under former I.R.C. § 30(a) for 1985) and the Base Amount is a direct function of historical QREs incurred during the statutory base years. Under the rolling base period rules of former I.R.C. § 30(c)(1) applicable in 1985, the base amount was the simple arithmetic average of QREs for the three preceding taxable years:
Base Amount1985 = (QREs1982 + QREs1983 + QREs1984) ÷ 3 (for Research, Inc.: ($1,426,165 + $1,772,137 + $1,857,538) ÷ 3 = $1,685,280)

Under the modern Regular Credit of I.R.C. § 41(c)(1) and (3), the base amount is the product of the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years and the fixed-base percentage (the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for the 1984–1988 base years):
Base Amount = Fixed-Base Percentage × Average Annual Gross Receipts4 preceding years, where Fixed-Base Percentage = Σ QREs1984–1988 ÷ Σ Gross Receipts1984–1988

As these equations demonstrate, the integrity of the incremental credit depends entirely on the definitional symmetry between QREscredit year and QREsbase period. If a taxpayer expands the scope of what it classifies as "qualified research" in the credit year—such as capturing custom engineering costs in "special system projects" that were previously treated as routine cost of goods sold or non-R&D overhead—while leaving the numerator of the base period fixed at its original, narrower scope, the resulting difference (QREscredit year − Base Amount) does not measure a real increase in research activity. Instead, it measures an accounting reclassification.

In Research, Inc., the taxpayer's claim presented precisely this problem. Before 1985, the taxpayer had claimed as QREs only those expenses related to its standard product line. In its amended return for fiscal year 1985, however, the taxpayer for the first time claimed an additional $1,667,717 of expenses associated with its "special system projects"—prototype systems designed and built to meet the specialized needs and requirements of individual customers. Although the taxpayer had engaged in developing "special system projects" in each of fiscal years 1982, 1983, and 1984, it did not adjust its base period expenses to reflect those projects and admitted that it could not do so. The District Court held that, without an accounting of the base period QREs attributable to both its unique and standard product lines, the taxpayer could not show the required increase in research expenditures over the base period average; finding the language of Section 30 clear, the court expressly declined to resort to analogous case law or to the IRS's unpublished, non-binding private rulings.
Catastrophic Record Destruction and Breach of IRC Section 6001

Once it was established that the taxpayer had engaged in "special system projects" in each base period year, Research, Inc. confronted an insurmountable evidentiary barrier: it had destroyed the relevant documentation of its qualified research expenses for 1982, 1983, and 1984, or was otherwise unable to produce it. Although the court decided the case on burden-of-proof grounds and its opinion does not cite I.R.C. § 6001 or Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, the same failure would today implicate those recordkeeping mandates.

In corporate tax administration, a frequent operational failure occurs when a corporation's general document retention policy is governed solely by the standard three-year federal statute of limitations for assessment under I.R.C. § 6501(a). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(e), however, books and records required to establish tax attributes must be retained "so long as the contents thereof may become material in the administration of any internal revenue law". Because the research tax credit requires the computation of a base amount derived from prior taxable years—whether the three preceding years under former I.R.C. § 30(c)(1) and current I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) (ASC), or the 1984–1988 base years under current I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(A)—historical records from otherwise "closed" tax years remain legally material in every subsequent open credit year.

When Research, Inc. could not produce its historical records for the "special system projects," it rendered itself incapable of fulfilling its affirmative burden of proving the correct amount of its base period research expenses—a burden the court grounded in Helvering v. Taylor, 293 U.S. 507 (1935), and Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, rather than in Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1 or Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), the latter of which postdates the decision. In tax refund litigation in a United States District Court or the United States Court of Federal Claims, the taxpayer bears a dual burden of proof: the taxpayer must prove not only that the IRS assessment was erroneous, but also establish the exact dollar amount of the overpayment to which it is entitled. Because the base period QREs are an indispensable variable in the statutory formula, the inability to substantiate the base period amount means the taxpayer cannot mathematically prove the amount of the credit.
Inapplicability of the Cohan Rule to Unsubstantiated Base Period Attributes

A critical legal takeaway from Research, Inc. v. United States—although the opinion itself never mentions the Cohan doctrine—is its rejection of an unsupported estimate of base period expenses: the taxpayer's $404,237 refund claim was predicated on a hypothecated upward adjustment of $396,801 to the base period expense figure, derived from a "sales ratio" calculated by the Government's examiner, and the court found no basis in law or fact for that adjustment. Subsequent federal case law, most recently George v. Commissioner, has likewise refused to rescue an unsubstantiated base period through judicial estimation under the Cohan doctrine. Originating in Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Cohan rule permits a court to approximate the amount of an allowable tax deduction or credit when the taxpayer establishes that it actually incurred a qualifying expense, but lacks exact records of the amount, bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of its own making.

However, in the context of the incremental research credit, the Cohan doctrine fails when applied to destroyed or missing base period records for two distinct legal reasons. First, under Cohan, a court may only estimate an expense if the record provides a reasonable, credible evidentiary foundation upon which to base the approximation; pure speculation or uncorroborated guesswork is prohibited. When a taxpayer claims "special system projects" that vary wildly in technical scope, custom engineering complexity, and commercial production overlap from year to year, and has destroyed all underlying project documentation for the base years, there is no reliable statistical or factual baseline from which to extrapolate the base period QREs. As the IRS notes in Exhibit D of its Research Credit computational issues guidance (citing Research, Inc., 95-2 USTC ¶ 50,407), a flat increase in amount or percentage from year to year may identify the use of estimates or extrapolations in applying the consistency rule, and failure to maintain sufficient records to accurately substantiate the base period expenditures may be grounds for disallowance of the claim.

Second, in a credit year calculation, applying Cohan to estimate QREs rewards the taxpayer by granting a minimum floor of expenses; in contrast, in a base period calculation, the taxpayer's interest is to minimize base period QREs to maximize the incremental credit. Allowing a taxpayer to destroy base period records and then rely on favorable estimates would create a perverse moral hazard, encouraging the spoliation of historical accounting records whenever base year R&D spending was high.

The continued relevance of this principle was illustrated in the U.S. Tax Court's memorandum opinion in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10. In George, which involved research credits claimed by George's of Missouri, Inc., a poultry producer, for its 2012 through 2014 tax years, the Tax Court found that contemporaneous documentation and credible testimony substantiated some, but not all, of the taxpayer's research trials, and it rejected the taxpayer's estimate of base period QREs for 2009 through 2011—derived by applying a ratio based on credit-year QREs—because the taxpayer failed to provide documentation sufficient to support an informed estimate. As a result, the Tax Court held that it was unable to apply the Cohan rule to estimate the missing base period QREs. Unlike the court in Research, Inc., however, the George court did not disallow the credit entirely: because the claim was computed under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) (codified at the time at I.R.C. § 41(c)(5), now § 41(c)(4)), the inability to substantiate the three-year rolling base period led the court to apply the statutory 6 percent rate (now I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)(B)) rather than the 14 percent incremental rate, allowing the taxpayer research credits despite its failure to substantiate the base period or address the consistency rule, whereas under the Regular Credit regime at issue in Research, Inc. (and in cases like United States v. Quebe), the inability to substantiate the base period resulted in a complete 100 percent disallowance of the research credit.
Cost Accounting and Technical Segregation Deficiencies in "Special System Projects"

Beyond the missing records, the facts of Research, Inc. v. United States—in which research expenses tied to customer-specific prototype systems were claimed for the first time years after the base period—illustrate a recurring technical and cost-accounting vulnerability in manufacturing and engineering enterprises: the failure to contemporaneously segregate qualified research activities from routine commercial production in hybrid, custom-engineered projects, although the court's brief opinion did not itself analyze the taxpayer's cost-accounting methods.

In standard financial accounting, companies maintain dedicated R&D cost centers (aligned with Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) ASC Topic 730, formerly SFAS No. 2) for pure new product development. For these dedicated departments, both credit-year and base-year expenses are tracked on the general ledger, making base period consistency straightforward. However, "special system projects"—bespoke engineering orders where a manufacturer designs and builds a specialized system to meet a client's unique functional specifications—are typically accounted for under job-order costing or Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) rather than R&D expense.

For an expenditure within a "special system project" to qualify as a QRE under current I.R.C. § 41(b), the underlying activity must satisfy the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), which was added by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and therefore did not govern Research, Inc.'s 1985 tax year. Under the Section 174 test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditure must be eligible for treatment as a research or experimental expenditure under I.R.C. § 174, meaning it represents research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). Crucially, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), costs of component materials, labor, or other elements involved in the actual construction, manufacture, or installation of depreciable property or commercial production units do not qualify. Under the technological in nature test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under the business component test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, improving function, performance, reliability, or quality. Finally, under the process of experimentation test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all—defined as at least 80 percent under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)—of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation, which requires a structured evaluation of alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error to resolve technological uncertainty.

Furthermore, under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H), activities conducted after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need, duplication of an existing business component, routine quality control testing, and funded research (where the taxpayer fails to retain substantial rights or bears no financial risk under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and § 1.174-2(b)(3)) are strictly excluded.

When a taxpayer retrospectively mines its job-costing records in a claim year to extract "special system projects" (arguing that specific custom orders involved genuine technological uncertainty and a process of experimentation rather than mere customer adaptation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(B)), it triggers an immediate consistency obligation. Because "special system projects" are heterogeneous—some orders require ground-up experimental engineering while others require only routine parameter configuration of existing designs—a general ledger summary of total "special system" revenue or COGS in the base period is useless. To satisfy the consistency requirement, the taxpayer must possess the exact project-level engineering specifications, customer contracts, and employee time-tracking logs from the base period years to evaluate each historical "special system project" under the exact same I.R.C. § 41(d) and § 174 criteria applied to the credit year. Because Research, Inc. was unable to produce any accounting of the base period QREs attributable to its "special system projects," its claim failed on summary judgment.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Research, Inc. v. United States into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic corporate taxpayers confronting the exact legal, computational, and evidentiary traps identified by the District of Minnesota. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial restructuring blueprint covering project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation cost tracking.
Case Study 1: Industrial Automation and Custom Thermal Processing Systems Manufacturer ("Special System Projects" Under the Regular and ASC Regimes)
Factual Scenario and Identified Pitfalls

Thermex Process Controls, Inc. ("Thermex") is a mid-market U.S. industrial equipment manufacturer specializing in high-intensity infrared radiant heating systems, curing ovens, and multi-zone digital power controllers used in aerospace composite curing and semiconductor wafer annealing. Thermex operates two distinct operational divisions. Its Standard Catalog Division designs and develops next-generation modular controllers and heating lamps; all engineering wages and prototype supplies for this division are booked directly to General Ledger Account 6400 (R&D Expense — ASC 730) and have been consistently claimed on IRS Form 6765 under the Regular Credit (I.R.C. § 41(a)(1)) since the 1984–1988 base period. Conversely, its Custom Engineered Systems Division ("Special System Projects") designs, engineers, fabricates, and installs bespoke, multi-megawatt thermal processing lines tailored to specific customer manufacturing plants. Accounting for 60 percent of company revenue, all engineering wages and materials for this custom division are booked to Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) under job-order cost accounting.

In 2026, Thermex engages an outside tax advisory firm to conduct a lookback R&D study for open tax years 2023, 2024, and 2025. The advisors propose capturing $4.2 million per year in previously unclaimed QREs from the Custom Engineered Systems Division ("Special System Projects"), arguing that roughly 35 percent of these custom orders require resolving fundamental thermodynamic and fluid-dynamics uncertainties through computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling and iterative prototype testing.

However, Thermex faces the exact multi-layered trap of Research, Inc. v. United States. First, regarding base period consistency and record destruction, Thermex performed custom "Special System Projects" during the 1984–1988 Regular Credit base period (as well as the 2020–2022 rolling base period if electing the ASC under I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)), but omitted them from its historical base computations. Worse, during a 2021 enterprise resource planning (ERP) migration and routine seven-year document purge, Thermex destroyed all paper job-folders from 1984–1988 and archived unindexed 2020–2021 timecards on legacy magnetic tape. Second, regarding the blur between adaptation and experimentation, the job-costing records for "Special System Projects" lump together initial experimental thermal modeling with routine computer-aided design (CAD) layout adjustments (excluded customer adaptation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(B)) and shop-floor assembly of the deliverable commercial oven (excluded production costs under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4)). Third, regarding funded research exposure, customer purchase orders for the "Special System Projects" utilize standard commercial terms containing milestone progress payments and ambiguous intellectual property clauses, creating a high risk that the IRS will disallow the projects as "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance & Base Period Record Retention Architecture

To avoid total disallowance of the Regular Credit under Research, Inc. v. United States (or forced application of the 6 percent rate under the ASC where base period QREs cannot be substantiated, as in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10), Thermex must immediately halt any claim under the Regular Credit that includes "Special System Projects" unless 1984–1988 records can be forensically recovered. Because the 1984–1988 paper job folders were permanently destroyed, Thermex cannot legally include "Special System Projects" under the Regular Credit without violating I.R.C. § 41(c)(5) [formerly § 41(c)(6)].

Instead, Thermex must execute a strategic election of the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) on timely filed original returns (or valid amended returns where permitted under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2) if the credit was not previously claimed on the original return), shifting the base period lookback from 1984–1988 to the three immediately preceding taxable years (for example, 2020–2022 for the 2023 credit year). Concurrently, Thermex must commission an information technology forensic recovery of the 2020–2022 legacy magnetic tapes, restoring all ERP job-cost ledgers, payroll registers, bill of materials (BOM) files, and engineering change notices (ECNs) for every "Special System Project" executed in the three-year rolling base period. Furthermore, the company must rescind its corporate seven-year destruction policy for engineering and cost-accounting records and institute a permanent corporate governance mandate under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(e). This mandate requires that all ERP project-costing tables, W-2 wage registers, general ledgers, customer contracts, and technical design repositories be preserved in an immutable, indexed cloud archive for at least as long as they remain material—covering the three-year ASC base period, the credit year, the three-year assessment statute, and the full period (up to 20 years under I.R.C. § 39(a)) during which any resulting credit carryforward may be used and examined, or permanently if any Regular Credit attributes are maintained. Finally, Thermex must establish an R&D Stage-Gate Committee, requiring every incoming "Special System Project" order to undergo a mandatory pre-engineering tax and technical classification review by the Vice President of Engineering, Cost Accounting Manager, and Tax Director prior to opening a job code in the ERP system.
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Four-Part Test Substantiation

To prevent the IRS from disqualifying the "Special System Projects" as routine customer adaptation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) or failing the "substantially all" process-of-experimentation standard articulated in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Thermex must standardize its contemporaneous technical documentation across both the restored base period projects and current credit year projects. Rather than defining the entire commercial curing oven line—which includes standard structural steel frames, conveyor belts, and commercial off-the-shelf programmable logic controllers—as the "business component" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), which would fail the 80 percent "substantially all" test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), Thermex must apply the regulatory "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) at the outset of each project. Technical documentation must explicitly isolate the specific sub-assembly or control algorithm (such as Sub-Assembly 04: Non-Uniform Quartz-Halogen Flux Array) as the discrete business component undergoing experimentation.

In tandem with shrinking-back the business component, Thermex must mandate that lead engineers complete a standardized Technical Uncertainty and Experimentation Charter within the Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) system before charging hours to an R&D sub-code. This charter must contemporaneously document why existing engineering knowledge, standard thermodynamic tables, and prior Thermex designs cannot achieve the target thermal uniformity tolerance—thereby proving technological uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and negating customer adaptation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(B)—alongside the specific scientific hypotheses formulated and the structured testing protocol. The PLM system must be configured to automatically version-control and timestamp every CFD simulation run, finite element analysis (FEA) mesh, failed thermal profile test log, and Engineering Change Order (ECO). Applying this exact technical screening rubric identically to the restored 2020–2022 base period projects and the 2023–2026 credit year projects establishes unimpeachable definitional symmetry under I.R.C. § 41(c)(5).
Step 3: Contract Terms & Statement of Work (SOW) Structuring

Because "Special System Projects" are performed under customer contracts, Thermex must restructure its commercial agreements to survive scrutiny under the funded research exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), ensuring compliance with Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), and Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1. Thermex must eliminate time-and-materials (T&M) billing or unconditional milestone payments for design phases, structuring all custom system contracts instead as firm fixed-price (FFP) agreements where payment is explicitly contingent upon the successful delivery and acceptance of a fully functional system passing quantifiable Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) at the customer's facility pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and § 1.174-2(b)(3). The contracts must include an explicit provision stating that if the system fails to meet the specified thermal uniformity tolerances during acceptance testing, the customer has the right to reject the system and receive a full refund of all prior progress deposits, placing the full financial risk of research failure squarely on Thermex.

Simultaneously, to satisfy the "substantial rights" mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), Thermex must revise its standard master supply agreements to bifurcate tangible equipment title from underlying intellectual property rights. While the customer receives title to the physical oven unit upon final acceptance, the contract must explicitly stipulate that Thermex retains exclusive ownership—or, at a minimum, a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free right to use, manufacture, and commercialize—all underlying inventions, thermodynamic models, control algorithms, and technical know-how developed during the project without paying any fee or seeking consent from the customer. Furthermore, the contractual Statement of Work (SOW) and internal Contract Line Item Numbers (CLINs) must be drafted to clearly separate Phase I: Experimental Subsystem Engineering & Prototype Validation from Phase II: Commercial System Fabrication, Assembly, and Site Installation.
Step 4: Experimentation & Base-to-Credit Year Cost Tracking

To eliminate the cost-accounting and substantiation failures illustrated by Research, Inc. and satisfy I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), Thermex must overhaul its ERP job-costing and time-tracking architecture by replacing single-bucket job codes with a mandatory multi-tiered Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), as detailed in the table below.

Case Study 2: Enterprise Cloud Infrastructure and Bespoke Systems Integration Provider (Post-M&A Base Period Reconstruction and Controlled Group Consistency)
Factual Scenario and Identified Pitfalls

AetherNet Cloud Solutions, Inc. ("AetherNet") is a U.S. enterprise software and hardware systems integrator that develops ultra-low-latency network switching firmware and distributed cloud telemetry platforms. Since its founding in 2015, AetherNet has claimed the federal R&D tax credit on its original Forms 1120 using the Regular Credit method (utilizing the start-up fixed-base percentage rules of I.R.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)), capturing only the wages of its core "Platform R&D Group". In January 2024, AetherNet acquired 100 percent of the stock of Vela Systems, Inc. ("Vela"), a specialized developer of custom high-frequency telemetry appliances. Both AetherNet and Vela maintain a "Special Systems Engineering Group" (SSEG) that builds custom-architected hardware-software integration solutions for tier-one financial and defense clients. Historically, neither AetherNet nor Vela included their SSEG divisions in their R&D tax credit calculations, viewing those groups as client-facing implementation teams.

For the 2025 and 2026 tax years, AetherNet's tax department decides to include the SSEG divisions of both AetherNet and Vela in its consolidated Form 6765 R&D credit claim, adding $6.8 million in annual wage and cloud-computing QREs. However, an internal pre-filing audit reveals three critical legal vulnerabilities directly governed by Research, Inc. v. United States and the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide. First, regarding controlled group aggregation and acquisition base adjustment failures, under I.R.C. § 41(f)(1) and § 41(f)(3)(A), all members of a controlled group of corporations are treated as a single taxpayer, and when a taxpayer acquires a major portion of a trade or business, the taxpayer's base period QREs and gross receipts must be increased by so much of the acquired business's historical QREs and gross receipts as is attributable to the portion acquired. AetherNet included Vela's 2025 and 2026 SSEG expenses in its credit year QREs, but failed to include either AetherNet's or Vela's historical SSEG expenses in the base period years. Second, regarding post-M&A spoliation of base period Agile and Jira records, following the January 2024 acquisition, AetherNet decommissioned Vela's legacy on-premise Jira ticketing server and Git code repositories covering tax years 2018 through 2022 to save licensing fees, retaining only high-level general ledger trial balances. Consequently, AetherNet cannot directly quantify how much time Vela's SSEG engineers spent on qualified experimentation versus routine client configuration during the base years. Third, regarding internal-use software risks, portions of the SSEG cloud telemetry tools are used internally by AetherNet to monitor client managed-services networks, triggering the stringent three-part "High Threshold of Innovation" test applicable to Internal-Use Software (IUS) under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance & Post-M&A Base Period Reconstruction Architecture

Under the principles of Research, Inc. v. United States and the modern consistency rule, if AetherNet includes the SSEG division in its 2025 and 2026 credit years while omitting SSEG expenses from its base period (or estimating Vela's historical SSEG base expenses via an unverified flat percentage), the IRS will disallow the claim for violating the consistency rule of I.R.C. § 41(c)(5) and the acquisition rules of I.R.C. § 41(f)(3). To remediate this exposure, AetherNet's legal and IT teams must first attempt to forensically recover Vela's decommissioned 2018–2022 Jira and Git databases from off-site disaster-recovery snapshots, escrow backups, or archived developer virtual machines. If those primary technical records are irretrievably lost, AetherNet cannot rely on oral testimony or arbitrary percentage estimates: Research, Inc., 1995 WL 560140, found no basis in law or fact for a "sales ratio" upward adjustment to base period expenses, and George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, declined to apply the Cohan doctrine to a ratio-based base period estimate unsupported by documentation. In the event of irretrievable loss of Vela's historical SSEG technical records, AetherNet must exercise strict compliance governance by either excluding Vela's SSEG division from the credit-year QREs for any calculation period in which those base years are active, or conservatively including 100 percent of Vela's historical SSEG department engineering wages (verified via surviving W-2 payroll registers and general ledger trial balances) in the base period numerator so that the Government cannot allege artificial base deflation.

To prevent recurrence in future transactions, AetherNet must institute a mandatory corporate M&A Tax Attribute Escrow Protocol requiring that, prior to closing any future corporate acquisition or disposition under I.R.C. § 41(f)(3), the Tax Department executes a Section 6001 Base Period Data Freeze. This governance protocol legally and technically prohibits IT integration teams from decommissioning any target company's ERP, payroll, time-tracking, Jira, Git, or contract repositories until a complete, indexed archival image covering all statutory base period years is extracted and verified by Tax Counsel.
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Four-Part / IUS Test Substantiation

To substantiate that the SSEG projects qualify under I.R.C. § 41(d) and survive Internal-Use Software (IUS) scrutiny across both base and credit years, AetherNet must restructure its software engineering documentation workflows. First, AetherNet must establish clear architectural and documentation boundaries under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) separating SSEG software developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third-party customers—or software that enables third parties to interact with AetherNet's hardware appliances—from software used solely for AetherNet's general and administrative (G&A) or internal network management functions. For any module subject to the IUS rules, engineering architects must complete a contemporaneous High Threshold of Innovation Memorandum prior to sprint execution. This memorandum must document innovativeness (demonstrated through a measurable, substantial reduction in latency or increase in throughput), significant economic risk (where substantial resources are committed and technical uncertainty prevents guaranteed recovery within a reasonable period), and commercial unavailability (proving that no existing commercial software could be purchased, leased, or licensed and used without modifications that themselves satisfy the first two prongs).

Second, AetherNet must configure Jira and GitHub Enterprise so that every SSEG development Epic cannot be initiated without mandatory metadata fields capturing the specific architectural or algorithmic uncertainty (such as kernel-bypass packet drop under non-uniform memory access loads), the alternative architectures evaluated (such as extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) versus custom field-programmable gate array (FPGA) offload), and direct links to automated benchmark test logs and failed pull requests demonstrating a systematic process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C).
Step 3: Contract Terms & Statement of Work (SOW) Structuring

To ensure SSEG client integration engagements are not disqualified as funded research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) or routine client configuration under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(B), AetherNet must standardize its Master Services Agreements (MSAs) and Statements of Work. Legal counsel must audit all SSEG client contracts to strike boilerplate "work-made-for-hire" or exclusive intellectual property assignment provisions that divest AetherNet of substantial rights under Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). These clauses must be replaced with a standardized intellectual property provision granting AetherNet sole ownership of all core firmware, telemetry protocols, and reusable software frameworks ("Background and Core Developed Technology"), while granting the client only a non-exclusive license to use the integrated system. Furthermore, AetherNet must convert SSEG development contracts from hourly staff-augmentation or T&M billing to fixed-price deliverable contracts tied to strict Service Level Objective (SLO) acceptance benchmarks, such as achieving sub-10-microsecond tail latency under a 100 Gbps load. The contracts must specify that AetherNet bears the sole financial cost of all engineering rework required to pass acceptance testing, and that non-conforming deliverables entitle the client to reject the system without payment obligation.
Step 4: Experimentation & Base-to-Credit Year Cost Tracking

To guarantee compliance with the consistency rule of I.R.C. § 41(c)(5) and the substantiation standards of Research, Inc. v. United States, AetherNet must integrate its Jira agile management platform directly with its payroll, timekeeping, and cloud-billing systems using the standardized classification structure set forth in the table below.

Whenever a cost category (such as Jira Category A SSEG wages or Cloud Tag: RD-Sim-PreProd computing costs) is included in the current credit year for any controlled group member, the ledger automatically pulls and locks the exact corresponding general ledger and Jira/cloud cost pools across all base period years for every predecessor and acquired entity, ensuring complete mathematical symmetry and permanent audit readiness.
Strategic Conclusions for R&D Tax Practice

The ruling in Research, Inc. v. United States, 95-1 USTC ¶ 50,407 (D. Minn. 1995), establishes an uncompromising legal boundary in United States tax administration: the federal R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41 is not a subsidy for the absolute volume of a taxpayer's engineering activities, but a strictly mathematical reward for verified incremental growth over a historical baseline. When taxpayers or their advisors retrospectively expand the scope of claimed QREs in an open tax year—particularly by reaching into non-traditional cost centers to capture custom-engineered "special system projects"—they trigger an immediate, non-negotiable statutory obligation under I.R.C. § 41(c)(5) [formerly § 41(c)(6)], enacted in 1989 to resolve the very problem presented in Research, Inc., to identify, quantify, and include identical project expenditures incurred during the base period.

As demonstrated by the taxpayer's defeat in Research, Inc., the destruction or absence of base period records can be fatal to a Regular Credit claim, and, as George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, illustrates, under the ASC it relegates the taxpayer to the reduced 6 percent rate. The Research, Inc. court found no basis in law or fact for an examiner's sales-ratio adjustment to base period expenses, the Tax Court in George declined to apply the Cohan rule where the taxpayer offered no documented basis for a reasonable estimate of base period QREs, and the IRS treats flat percentage extrapolations as a signal of estimated or asymmetrical base period computations. To withstand IRS examination and judicial review, corporate taxpayers must align their document retention policies with the multi-year materiality mandate of I.R.C. § 6001, enforce strict project-level cost accounting that separates I.R.C. § 174 experimentation from commercial production and customer adaptation, and maintain symmetrical technical and financial substantiation across both base and determination years.
